newsitem.title: USA: GE earnings seen casting bright glow.
newsitem.headline: GE earnings seen casting bright glow.

text.p: The earnings outlook for General Electric Co is casting a warm glow over investors, despite rising competition in GE's 12 areas of operations, analysts said on Monday.
The Fairfield, Conn.-based company is expected to announce its fourth-quarter 1996 earnings by the end of this week.
GE is set to post the highest net income of any U.S. company when its projected $7.25 billion annual net, or $4.40 a share, pushes it past General Motors Corp, analysts said.
GE's market capitalization of $168 billion is the highest of any company in the world, a peak it reached for the first time last year, when it surpassed Royal Dutch/Shell Group of Cos, analysts said.

According to First Call, which monitors Wall Street analysts' earnings projections, GE's earnings per share for the fourth quarter of 1996 are expected to be $1.26, up 12.5 percent from the same period a year ago.
"We think we're positioned to announce very strong results and we'll let that announcement speak for itself," GE spokesman Bruce Bunch told Reuters. He did not elaborate.
Analysts credited GE's growth to shrewd acquisitions and overseas expansion, coupled with a company-wide drive for production quality-control and forays into the services area.
"The amazing thing about General Electric is that this late in the economic cycle, they're accelerating rather than decelerating their growth," said Jeanne Terrile, an analyst at Merrill Lynch.
"They are one company that has really managed to make diversity work," said Steve O'Neil, vice president at J.J.B. Hilliard, W.L. Lyons Inc in Louisville.
"They are relentless in terms of pursuing productivity improvement, cost-reductions and quality-control and they're moving aggressively into services in a number of areas."
The services area enjoys higher margins than traditional manufacturing, said O'Neil.
A key element in GE's growth is the financial clout of General Electric Captial Services Inc, which last year had $185 billion in assets, $26.5 billion in revenues and $2.4 billion in net income.
"GE is an opportunistic acquirer of companies and, with their financial strength, they have the ability to make sizable acquisitions," said O'Neil.

Analysts said GE's was so diverse that, even if a slowing economy affected certain businesses like appliances, electric motors and plastics, it could be offset by longer-cycle businesses such as aircraft engines and power systems.
One of the few potential clouds on the horizon for GE, which owns American network NBC, is broadcasting, said an analyst.
"I'm keeping an eye on NBC in 1997. There will be a point at which NBC's growth will slow down a little bit and the question is whether it will be in 1997," she said.
"Right now, NBC is at the top of its game and is doing extremely well, but there is a certain amount of economic and creative cyclicality in the broadcast business."
But the analyst added that GE's earnings outlook was generally bright, with 1997 earnings expected to be in the $4.90-4.95 range and 1998 earnings around $5.60.
"In 1997, GE is the place to be, regardless of what the market does," she said. "If the market is down, GE ought to be a good place to hide, because whatever else it has, it has a lot of liquidity."
